prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock: Katori's magic-wavelength concept and its realisation, with Ye's demonstration of many-atom clocks at the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep B019 as a single-part, two-name prize and my position has not changed after the full exchange. The chair asks what is discovered beyond better numbers. My answer: it is a new way of measuring. Katori's magic-wavelength condition removes the first-order lattice light shift, which breaks the old trade-off between long interrogation time and perturbation by the trapping light, and it lets many atoms be read out in parallel with Doppler and recoil effects suppressed. That is a change of kind, because the statistical gain from N atoms and the cancelled systematic arrive together, and the instrument becomes limited by many-body physics (collisional and lattice-induced shifts, Fermi-gas effects) rather than by single-particle control. Ye's group then showed what the idea can deliver: systematic budgets and clock-clock stability at the 10^-18 level, with the gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres. The evidence is the kind I trust most as an experimentalist. The result is reproduced and compared across JILA, RIKEN, SYRTE, PTB and NIST with agreed uncertainty budgets, and it is already used for tests of constancy of constants and dark-matter searches. As the chair and Danielsson say, and I agree, the citation should rest on the instrument and its physics, and the pending redefinition of the second should stay out of the citation and the scientific rationale. Five of eight members prefer this configuration and all name the same pair, but I do not rely on that count. I rely on the fact that none of the objections raised in round 1 disputes the experimental result.
statement.case_against: The overlap objection has not gone away and I do not dismiss it. The comb (2005), single-particle control (2012) and laser cooling (1997, 2018) are all honoured, and a committee could still read the lattice clock as the end of a long, honourable refinement of precision spectroscopy. I think the magic-wavelength argument answers this, but it is a judgment on which Mehlig and Olsson may reasonably differ and I cannot prove it. Credit is also not closed: priority for the first Sr lattice clock (Tokyo, JILA, SYRTE) rests on my recall of the record, and I have not seen a verified priority record. Lemonde, Derevianko on magic-wavelength theory and shifts, and ion-clock groups with competing accuracy records are outside the names. A prize that put the clock in the citation but left several strong clock groups out would be criticised, and that risk is real. Finally, several supporters moved to B019 only after reading the other ballots, so its support is partly a consolidation and not independent convergence.

responses.point: Mehlig regards B019 as an instrument achievement on top of the frequency comb, whereas B047 is a new regime of matter, but would not object if the committee preferred B019 for maturity.
responses.response: I understand the distinction, but I think the line between instrument and discovery is less sharp in measurement physics than in condensed matter. A clock at 10^-18 is a probe that shows the redshift across a millimetre and constrains drifts of constants, which no earlier clock could do, and the many-body shifts in a lattice clock are physics in themselves. I accept that B047 opens a larger new regime. My reservation about B047 is not that the phases are unreal, since they are reproduced, but that the claim being rewarded is still moving: the pairing mechanism is unsettled and twist-angle disorder limits quantitative comparison. I take your willingness not to object as helpful, and I would ask you to weigh maturity as heavily as breadth.

responses.point: Olsson would not oppose B019 if the committee settles that Katori's magic wavelength is the original discovery and not a refinement of earlier metrology, but places the broader opening for new physics with the moire platform.
responses.response: That is the right test, and I think the record passes it. The magic-wavelength proposal came in 2001 and the first Sr lattice-clock demonstration followed in 2003, and neither the comb nor the ion-trap work contains that idea. The comb counts the cycles and the ion work shows how to control one particle, while the lattice clock cancels a systematic that is specific to trapping many neutral atoms. On the broader opening, I agree that B047 is the stronger case for new physics. I would not oppose it in a later cycle, and I list it first among my alternatives. For this cycle, B019 has settled attribution and reproducibility, whereas B047 still has the Cao and Fatemi experimental credit gap that a three-name limit cannot close.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the citation state that the concept and first demonstration are Katori's, so the prize does not read as a prize for accuracy records alone.
responses.response: I accept your point and have changed the citation wording accordingly. It now names Katori's magic-wavelength concept and its realisation first, and credits Ye's group for demonstrating many-atom clocks at the 10^-18 level. This keeps the prize on the idea and the instrument and not on the record number. I still would not extend the names to theory. Derevianko and Lemonde contributed, but I read the decisive step as the experimental demonstration that the magic condition works and delivers the accuracy. I do share your wish for a priority check on the first lattice-clock measurements.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B017 as the first alternative and not as a second prize part, because a two-topic AMO prize would need a clear split of the three names, and he says the redefinition of the second is still prospective.
responses.response: I agree on both points. I have dropped B017 as a second part: a split would need four names (Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller) or would force a cut that I cannot justify, and the 2001 BEC and 1997 and 2018 cooling prizes make a second AMO part harder. I keep it as an alternative only. On the second, I agree that the redefinition belongs outside the citation. If it comes up in the public rationale at all, it should appear only as a consequence of the instrument, never as the reason for the prize. I also support your question about an outside check of the Sr priority record, since that is the one place where a dispute could arise.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B012 for its stable interpretation and more than fifteen years of independent confirmation, and lists B019 as an alternative.
responses.response: I agree that stability of interpretation and long independent confirmation are the right properties to weigh, and the QSH effect has them. But B019 now meets the same test: more than fifteen years of independent comparison across five national and university laboratories, with a systematic budget that has been cross-checked in clock comparisons and not merely asserted. B012 has the attribution problem that you acknowledge yourself. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised, Zhang has died, and the 3D pioneers are not in the names. A citation limited to the 2D effect would be coherent, but it would leave out the theorists most responsible for the material route. B019 does not have an equivalent gap among its two proposed names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as the end of a line already honoured in 1997, 2005, 2012 and 2018. This is a judgment and I cannot settle it with evidence.

Priority between Katori's group, JILA and SYRTE for the first Sr lattice clock, and whether Lemonde or Derevianko should be recognised. My dates (2001 proposal, 2003 first demonstration) are from recall and not from a verified source.
The accuracy figures and the list of confirming laboratories are also from recall, not a verified source. I would ask for an outside check before the final ballot.
Whether B047 is mature enough: if the pairing mechanism were resolved I would weigh it more favourably.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with B019 or its credited names. I am on the WACQT management team (Chalmers-led), which overlaps institutionally with Johansson's home and with the superconducting-circuit work behind B004, so I would recuse on B004 if it advanced; it is not in my preferred configuration. My own work is on rare-earth-ion quantum memories and ultrasound optical tomography, and I am on the management team of Deep Light Vision. None of these concern B019, B047 or B017. I have no personal link to Katori or Ye.
